newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche says revamp will boost 97 earnings.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche says revamp will boost 97 earnings.

text.p: Deutsche Bank, fighting to cut domestic costs, said on Wednesday it had finished a reorganisation that would boost earnings from retail banking, private banking and unit trusts by over 10 percent in 1997.

Profits would benefit from a revamp over the last three years in which Deutsche shed staff, reorganised its branch network and won new customers, for example by moving into telephone banking and discount brokerage, the bank said.

Underscoring the overhaul, Deutsche said it had given its private clients division a new structure with four areas of management responsibility -- customer service, new sales outlets and administration, marketing, and private banking for wealthy clients.

The new structure reflected the bank's drive to free its 1,700 domestic branches from administrative tasks which were being pooled in regional centres, enabling branch staff to concentrate more on serving customers.

"We expect this to lead to a considerable double-digit percentage rise in earnings this year," Georg Krupp, a management board member who shares responsibility for Private Clients, told a news conference.

With the changes in place, the division had a "very good chance" of reaching a pre-tax return on equity of 25 percent in the coming years, the target Deutsche has set for the group as a whole, Krupp said.

Analysts said that excluding Deutsche's profitable investment fund business, grouped in subsidiary DWS, the bank earned only a meagre return on equity in its retail banking business of well below 10 percent before tax.
In recent years Deutsche, like most of its major domestic rivals, had undergone a cultural revolution to woo clients by becoming more accessible and customer-friendly.
It has set up a telephone banking subsidiary, Bank 24, extended branch opening hours and late last year opened two branches in supermarkets, called "bankingshops."
Burkhardt Pauluhn, who heads the new sales outlets and administration department, said the bankingshops were performing well, with particularly strong interest from homebuyers on Saturday afternoons.
Pauluhn said Deutsche had already reached agreements with further retailers and would have a total of 10 bankingshops by the summer in various supermarkets, including one in Berlin.

Krupp stressed the bank did not plan to shed staff who dealt directly with customers because that would impair its service. But the bank saw scope to merge administrative centres in the coming years. He said it was hard to predict the scale of job cuts this would entail.

"To quote an adage, to cut the branches can kill the tree," Krupp said, adding that 80 to 85 percent of customers in Germany still preferred contact with their local branch to telephone banking. "If you shed branches excessively you run the risk of losing your customers."

Deutsche said creating a separate management layer for marketing was unprecedented in a German bank and highlighted its intention to sell its products more aggressively, for example by approaching customers by telephone and seeking more client feedback.
Deutsche is setting up its own call centre to answer general questions about the bank and coordinate telephone marketing drives.

The bank also announced it had increased its stake in Bankhaus Grunelius KG, a private bank, to 100 percent from 83.4 percent previously. Grunelius will coordinate Deutsche's private banking services for wealthy clients in Germany.
